title: He wasn't a danger to anyone ... charges should be laid: Deborah, Paul Boyd's sister
subtitle: Nearly five years after Paul Boyd's death at the hands of Vancouver police Const. Lee Chipperfield,
article: Nearly five years after Paul Boyd's death at the hands of Vancouver police Const. Lee Chipperfield, his older sister Deborah says the family is hoping "the truth" will finally win out.
She said in an emotional interview that the video that has suddenly surfaced showing the final moments of the 39-year-old animator's life may finally help set the record straight.
"All everyone has heard is that the police responded to a call of a man swinging a bike chain," the 46-year-old said Wednesday.
"This is TOTALLY untrue. That is not what they were initially responding to ..."
Her eyes welled and she composed herself.
It has been a roller-coaster since Thursday, when she learned a Winnipeg man had turned the footage over to the CBC.
Her "little" brother, who stood six-foot-four, grew up on the west side, the son of a mathematician and a nurse. He was friendly, intelligent, humorous and compassionate.

"Always drawing from the moment he was three," sis recalled, her eyes misting. "In his teen years he filled his books with doodles and drawings, his caricatures of teachers [at Lord Byng high school] got him in trouble, he did the cover of the yearbook the year he graduated."
Boyd started UBC intending to be an engineer until his dad David and Deborah helped him move and discovered his art work.
"He figured he'd never make a living from art so we said, no way. He went into fine arts, went to McGill, but he was a self-taught animator. That was his passion."
Boyd wasn't diagnosed until his early 20s with the bipolar disorder that precipitated his killing.
If you met him when he was well, you might never have guessed his condition.
"He was just like you or I - he was great with kids. It was a shame he didn't have the opportunity to be a dad."
But there were times, too, when Paul struggled with severe bouts of delusions, mania and depression - afraid unknown people were after him or spying on him.
Nevertheless, over the last 15 years he forged a successful career working for several different animation studios and teaching at the Vancouver Film School.
"He was such a courageous guy," Deborah said of his ability to recover and not let his illness define his life.
"It's hard to sum him up in a single moment."
Her emotions are still raw, the spasms of memory and grief difficult to control. She wished people knew him as she did.
"Hopefully this new evidence will finally bring some justice," Deborah said of the images tourist Andreas Bergen captured in Vancouver and forgot about until recently.

On August 13, 2007, at about 9:30 p.m., Chipperfield shot Boyd eight times near the corner of Granville and West 15th Avenue - the final fatal bullet delivered to the head of the wounded, unarmed man.
The dramatic and heart-rending 49-second video shows Boyd after the initial fusillade, hit seven times in the torso, painfully crawling across the street to his death.
Constable Mark Baird, Chipperfield's partner, can be seen removing the chain and bicycle lock. He later told the inquest he shouted: "Hold your fire."
Twenty-three seconds after that first volley, Chipperfield fired the coup de grace.
It's excruciating to watch.
"I wasn't surprised," Deborah said sadly.

"I had heard it all at the inquest. But it's like words don't matter. People don't believe it unless they see it. Witnesses said he was on his hands and knees, they said he was crawling but all Chipperfield had to do was say Paul was standing, that he was threatening. It didn't matter what anyone else said. Even the other officer said he was crawling. All that mattered was what Chipperfield said."
She paused before continuing bitterly.
"What did they call it, 'inattentive blindness'?" she acidly asked.
The Alberta Serious Incident Response Team was assigned Tuesday to review the case since the video cast a pall over the previous inquiries into what happened that night.
"I believe the ineptitude of the police actually caused this whole tragic event," Deborah said, anger replacing grief.

"Did you know that the first two officers on the scene had originally approached him as a witness? That he wasn't doing anything but sitting calmly at a bus stop with another man? Did you know that one of the two officers pulled a gun on him, and had him face down on the ground complying with them? But their failure to follow proper procedure gave him the opportunity to jump up and pull a bicycle chain out of his backpack."
She was incensed again, as if it all happened yesterday, as if a scab had been ripped off.
"All of this came out in the coroner's inquest," she fumed.
"It didn't make any difference."
Still, Boyd that evening was in the throes of paranoia.
He was off his meds, yelling at strangers and attracting attention.
Had the officers who first approached him had mental-health training, Deborah thought the tragedy could have been prevented.
She would like to see better training for police - one of the nine recommendations of the inquest jury in December 2010.

But mostly Deborah is hoping this is a chance to change people's perception of her brother, a gentle giant of a man, a talented man with a wide circle of friends ... his sister can still hear him laugh.
"People have this image of him as a wild person swinging a chain ... He was such a loving man. He gave my son piggybacks, hung him upside down, made my daughter laugh ..."
She choked back her pain.

"I think of him playing with my two children," she said, her voice cracking. "They weren't afraid of him. He was just having a bad period in his life. His mother was dying. He wasn't a danger to anyone."
